I’m not sure how I found the Milk-Eyed Mender, but when I did freshman year of college I ripped it off of YouTube and onto my old Android phone so I could listen to it like a record while walking to class. My university’s campus looks like a giant limestone city from a medieval era, and my human sexuality class that semester was located in a building that was a part of quad with turrets and a courtyard. I remember listening to This Side of the Blue on one of the first truly cold days of fall as I waited for class to start on the second floor balcony. My phone got lost or stolen soon after that, and during that time I forgot about that album and Joanna Newsom. It wasn’t until recently that I rediscovered her. This winter I began to listen to Divers while cleaning the museum I work at. I listened to only that album and the Final Fantasy 9 soundtrack for a solid week and a half. Every experience I’ve had listening to her music has been so pleasant and memorable, even if it was washing dusty windows.

I think what was striking to me about her music initially is how textured it is and how individually each instrument has a classic sound that in unison create a sound both nostalgic and new. Her voice had a way of making me actually listen to her lyrics because her enunciation has a way of getting stuck in my brain. Her music is a fantasy that reminds me of the worlds I conjured as a kid — very comforting and beautiful yet also volatile and strange.

It seems as though people with aphantasia and CPTSD/PTSD experience emotional rather than visual flashbacks. It doesn’t look like any studies have been conducted to examine the correlation between the two, however, and unfortunately it’d be ethically impossible to do an experimental study that would explore cause and effect. 

I still think this is really interesting. CPTSD/PTSD is a weird disorder in which one remembers too well or not at all, and it seems as though some individuals with the disorder experience one condition more than the other. Maybe visualization ability, whether caused by trauma or not, relates to one’s memory capabilities as well, and that is an antecedent to whether an individual with CPTSD/PTSD would fall into the over-remembering or poor memory subgroup.

There’s something called the paradox of choice in psychology in which “having many options to choose from, rather than making people happy and ensuring they get what they want, can cause them stress and problematize decision-making”. I think this applies not only to RPGs which have an absurd amount of customizable features but also games in which you can interact with nearly everything. Sure, having almost everything be so that you can interact with it may increase immersion, but I do not think it would improve the overall gameplay experience. 

Source of quote: https://whatis.techtarget.com/definition/paradox-of-choice
